slides.title: FUSE
items: RACK
Shared fuse inventory for regional utilities
Illustrative seed pitch

slides.title: A blown fuse should not strand a feeder.
items: Crews already carry common cartridge sizes. What they lack is a shared count of what the neighboring yard still holds.
Fuse Rack pools spare stock across districts so a night truck can pull a verified cartridge before the feeder sits cold.

slides.title: The bay keeps the count
items: Each bay scans a cartridge into a shared bin. The next crew sees live counts before leaving the yard.
A sealed bag travels with a lot number. The receiving bay confirms the amp rating before the truck rolls.

slides.title: Pull, confirm, replace
items: 01 Pull
The night lead selects a cartridge from the shared rack against the feeder ticket.
02 Confirm
A second tech verifies amp rating and lot number before the seal is broken.
03 Replace
The empty slot is marked pending restock. The shared count drops in the same minute.

slides.title: Outage minutes the shared rack avoids
items: Illustrative feeder model • minutes of cold time avoided after a blown cartridge
At twelve shared spares, modeled cold time falls from 94 to 28 minutes. The gain comes from skipping a cross-town parts run.

slides.title: Unit economics of a shared bay
items: $18k / year
Subscription per participating bay for inventory software, sealed bags and quarterly audits.
$11.2k direct
Bag software $4.1k, bagging and seals $2.4k, audit labor $4.7k. Contribution $6.8k before head-office overhead.

slides.title: Start with one corridor
items: 36 bays
Assume each bay avoids two cross-town runs a month. At $420 per avoided run, corridor savings are $362,880 before subscription fees.
Pilot rule
Open a corridor only when three adjacent yards can each commit twelve common cartridge SKUs.

slides.title: Why share the rack?
items: Local stock
Fast for familiar faults. Thin for rare amp ratings that sit idle for months.
Central warehouse
Deep assortment, but every night run pays the drive before the feeder is restored.
Shared bay
A verified cartridge in a neighboring yard. The truck leaves with a counted spare.

slides.title: Two leads own the count
items: Rafi Cole / inventory
Rafi owns SKU standards, sealed-bag lots and the quarterly audit. A disputed count freezes the SKU until both bays sign.
Nia Park / night ops
Nia owns feeder tickets and truck dispatch. Her team will not leave without a confirmed amp rating on the bag tag.

slides.title: Ninety days on one corridor
items: Days 1–30
Instrument three bays. Photograph every shared SKU and seal the first lots.
Days 31–60
Run night pulls against live counts. Target fewer than two count disputes per week.
Days 61–90
Prove a 40% cut in cross-town parts runs before opening a second corridor.

slides.title: Stock the first corridor.
items: $4.8M seed
$2.1M for bay hardware and seals, $1.5M for inventory software, $1.2M for ops hiring and audits. Illustrative company and figures.
Target: 36 instrumented bays and a 40% cut in cross-town runs within 12 months.
